# Anaṅgaṇa Sutta (MN 5 (PTS MN i 24))

**ID:** MN 5 (PTS MN i 24)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Anaṅgaṇa Sutta
**PTS:** MN i 24

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Anaṅgaṇa Sutta* (MN 5) is a discourse delivered by the Venerable Sāriputta in dialogue with Mahāmoggallāna on the nature of "blemishes" (*aṅgaṇa*), defined as the sway of evil, unwholesome wishes [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Rogell 2003]. The sutta examines four classes of individuals based on whether mental blemishes are present or absent and whether the practitioner accurately recognizes their own condition [Edo Shonin et al. 2015; Anālayo 2014]. Sāriputta emphasizes that honest awareness of one's defiled or undefiled state is critical for making an effort to emerge from defilements or nurture purity [Edo Shonin et al. 2015; Anālayo 2014]. This instruction is illustrated by the simile of a bronze utensil purchased at a market that is either soiled or clean and either tended and polished or neglected [Anālayo 2014]. The discourse also discusses those who go forth not out of faith but for a livelihood, characterizing them with terms such as *unnala* ("haughty" or "insolent") [Levman 2014]. At the conclusion, Moggallāna praises Sāriputta's teaching, comparing the joyful reception of the Dhamma to a youth placing a fresh garland of flowers upon their head [Piya Tan 2002; Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Anālayo 2014].

In later Theravāda exegetical literature, Buddhaghosa's commentary on the sutta (*Majjhimanikāye Mūlapaṇṇāsa-aṭṭhakathā*) is well known for citing an earlier verse from an unidentified source establishing the doctrine of two truths: conventional (*sammuti*) and ultimate (*paramattha*) [Ñāṇananda 1971; Walshe 1987; Levman 2014].

Curated full parallels in Chinese Āgamas comprise *Madhyama-āgama* MĀ 87, *Ekottarika-āgama* EĀ 25.6, and an individual translation, T 49 (*Qiuyu jing*, 求欲經) [Anālayo 2016]. DharmaNexus independently confirms these parallels, reporting substantial cross-language alignments with T 49, MĀ 87, and EĀ 25.6 [DharmaNexus]. Comparative analysis highlights minor variations across these versions: for instance, while MN 5 and EĀ 25.6 mention either a boy or a girl receiving the flower garland, MĀ 87 and T 49 mention only a woman [Anālayo 2016]. DharmaNexus also records extensive Pali-internal text reuse with collections including the *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22), the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* (AN 4, AN 5, AN 10), and other Majjhima discourses such as MN 77 and MN 105 [DharmaNexus].
